title: How Nutmeg Bought Manhattan
fullText: Somewhere in your kitchen right now, there is probably a small jar of nutmeg wedged between the cinnamon and the black pepper. The kind of thing you reach for maybe twice a year. It costs a few dollars. It has sat in your spice rack for months, maybe years, mostly forgotten except at the holidays. You would never guess that this exact spice once caused a genocide. You would never guess that a European empire once traded away the island that would become New York City just to control it. For most of human history, [music] this brown powder in your kitchen came from exactly one place on Earth and only one place. That fact alone was enough to start wars. Here is what almost nobody tells you. The nutmeg tree myristica fragrance is not native to Indonesia in general, not to Asia in general, not to any large land mass at all. For most of its existence on this planet, it grew wild on a tiny cluster of volcanic islands smaller than most cities. Surrounded by deep ocean, thousands of miles from Europe, reachable only after months at sea through waters most sailors of the era had never charted. Every nutmeg that reached a European table for thousands of years came from that one archipelago. Nowhere else on Earth had the right volcanic soil, the right rainfall, the right conditions. Nature had accidentally created a monopoly and human beings would spend centuries killing each other over it. This is the story of how a spice from 10 square miles of volcanic rock built the first corporate empire on Earth. It is the story of a massacre that erased an entire [music] people in under 10 weeks. A real estate swap that accidentally created modern New York. and a spice still tangled up today in poison, hallucination, and prison contraband. To understand any of it, you [music] have to start with a group of islands almost nobody could find on a map, thousands of miles from anywhere, a European of the time would have called civilization. Long before Europeans knew nutmeg existed, it was already moving along ancient trade [music] networks. Passed hand-to- hand from Bandanese traders to Javanese merchants to Indian and Arab middlemen, and finally to Venice, where it sold for staggering prices. Roman writers mentioned aromatic spices [music] from the far east centuries earlier. Though it is unclear how much genuine nutmeg [music] reached the Mediterranean that early since so much of what traveled the ancient [music] spice routes arrived blended, relabeled or outright counterfeited by the time it changed hands a dozen times. By the time of Marco Polo in the 13th century, nutmeg [music] was known well enough across Europe and the Islamic world to appear in medical texts, valued for [music] supposed healing properties as much as for flavor. Arab traders guarded the secret of its true origin for centuries, [music] inventing elaborate stories about dangerous seas, giant birds, and enchanted forests guarding the source. anything to protect their markup and keep European buyers from ever finding the islands themselves. Medieval Europeans knew the taste of nutmeg intimately. They had no idea it came from a real place at all. Everything changed in 1512 when Portuguese ships under Antonio de Abro became the first Europeans to sail into the Banda Sea and see the source with their own eyes. What they found were low volcanic islands [music] thick with evergreen trees. Each one hanging with a pale yellow fruit that split open to reveal a lacelike red covering wrapped around a dark seed. That covering became the spice mace. The seed inside, dried and ground, became nutmeg. A single tree could produce both spices at once, which meant the islands were sitting on two fortunes instead of one. The word itself traces back to Latin, nuk mosharta, the musky nut, filtered through old French into English as nutmeg. For the first time, Europe had found the source of one of its most expensive luxuries. And within a generation, every major European maritime power wanted a piece of it. But there was a problem. The nutmeg tree would not grow anywhere else. Transplanted seedlings died. Cutings failed. The specific volcanic [music] chemistry of the Bander Islands could not be replicated. And for two more centuries, nobody in the world figured out how to break [music] that dependence. Whoever controlled these 10 small islands controlled the entire global supply of nutmeg permanently by accident of geology. There was a second problem too, just as stubborn as the first. Nutmeg seeds lose their ability to sprout within days of leaving the fruit far faster than the seeds of most other spice bearing plants known to European traders at the time. You could not simply pocket a handful and carry them home across a year-long voyage. Anyone hoping to start a rival plantation elsewhere needed fresh, [music] viable seed, planted almost immediately, something no European ship crossing half the globe could realistically pull off, no matter how carefully the cargo was packed or stored below deck. The Bandanese people who actually lived there had already solved problems Europeans hadn't even considered. Long before any Portuguese ship arrived, they had developed careful drying and curing techniques to keep nutmeg and mace stable across months of sea travel to Java, India, and beyond. Techniques refined over generations and passed down as closely guarded family knowledge. They ran their own trading network, dealing directly with Chinese, Arab [music] and Malay merchants, setting their own prices and choosing their own trading partners, becoming genuinely wealthy in the process [music] with fine houses and imported goods to show for it. It was by most accounts a prosperous and largely self-governing society of free traders, not a primitive outpost waiting to be discovered. And visiting merchants from across Asia treated bander leaders as equals in negotiation, [music] not as subjects to be managed. By the time Europeans reached the source directly, nutmeg was already selling in European markets at markups approaching 6,000% over what it cost on Bander itself. The Bandines knew exactly how valuable their islands were. And after centuries of profitable trade with half of Asia, they had no intention of handing that value over to a handful of new arrivals from the other side of the world. This is the part most people never learn. In609, a Dutch fleet arrived to negotiate a trade monopoly with the bander's leaders called Orurankaya. Negotiations collapsed into violence and Band fighters killed the Dutch commander and dozens of his men. Among the survivors who escaped that bloody encounter was a young Dutch official named Jan Peter Zun Cohen. He never forgot it. Over the next 12 years, Cohen rose to become governor general of the Dutch East India Company, the VOCC. And he carried that grudge the entire way up. In 1621, Cohen got his chance. He sailed into Bander with 13 transport ships, over 1,600 soldiers, Japanese mercenaries, and enslaved laborers. and he gave the population of roughly 15,000 people a choice. Abandon their homeland or face annihilation. When they refused, Cohen ordered the killing to begin. Dutch forces and their mercenaries hunted down the island's leaders, tortured [music] and executed dozens of them in public, and then turned on the general population. Moving from village to village with a methodical efficiency [music] that survivors later described as almost business-like, as though the massacre itself was simply another logistics operation to be completed on schedule. In a matter of weeks, close to 3,000 Bandines were killed [music] outright. and close to 2,000 more were enslaved and deported. Thousands died of starvation and disease as their villages burned. A civilization that had thrived on that archipelago for centuries ceased to exist in under [music] 10 weeks. Here's the thing that made this more than just cruelty. Cohen wasn't simply taking revenge. He was solving a business problem the only way he knew [music] how. Applying the same cold logic a company today might apply to a supply chain bottleneck. Except the bottleneck in this case was a living population of 15,000 [music] people. With the band gone, the VOC brought in Dutch settlers and enslaved workers from across the archipelago to run nutmeg plantations under a strict lease system called the Perkaneer system, where former company soldiers were granted land [music] in exchange for delivering fixed quotas of nutmeg back to the company at a price the company itself decided. Total control of the land meant total control of the supply. Total control of the supply meant the VOC could set the price of nutmeg anywhere it wanted, anywhere in the world with no competition at all. Investors back in Amsterdam, who had bought shares in the VOC, saw dividends that regularly exceeded 20% a year, decade after decade, an almost unheard of return built directly on top of a depopulated archipelago. Within a generation, [music] the VOCC became the richest corporation in human history, worth more in today's terms than most modern tech giants combined. And Nutmeg was one of the small handful of commodities that made it possible. And the company protected that monopoly ruthlessly. Nutmeg trees found growing outside the VOCC's controlled plantations were chopped down and burned on site. [music] No exceptions. Every nutmeg shipped out for sale was deliberately coated in lime, not to preserve it, but to kill its ability to germinate if anyone tried to plant it elsewhere. VOC ships patrolled the surrounding waters to intercept smugglers, and severe penalties, sometimes death, [music] awaited anyone caught cultivating nutmeg without direct company authorization. Company inspectors periodically [music] tooured every plantation on the islands, counting trees against official registers, and any tree that appeared without a corresponding entry was destroyed immediately. No questions asked about how it might have gotten there. For nearly two centuries, this single company controlled the entire global nutmeg supply from a handful of tiny islands most of the world had never heard of, and it priced accordingly. A spice that cost almost nothing to grow on Bander soil could sell in London or Amsterdam for sums that would bankrupt an ordinary household for a single pound of it. And buyers had no alternative supplier to turn to [music] anywhere on the planet. There was just one thorn left in the Dutch side. One small bander island called Run, barely two miles long and less than a mile wide, remained under British control, garrisoned by a small English East India Company outpost that refused to budge. The two empires fought over that speck [music] of land for decades in skirmishes and blockades stretching across roughly four years. Each side convinced the other's presence there threatened the entire regional monopoly. Finally, in 1667, exhausted by war on multiple fronts, the Dutch and British signed the treaty of Brada. The Dutch offered a trade. Give us run and we will give you our claim to a swampy fur trading outpost on the other side of the world, a place called New Amsterdam. The Dutch, convinced nutmeg was worth far more than a swampy fur trading outpost, pushed hard for the trade. The British, worn down by years of war and already holding Manhattan by force, agreed to make it official. That outpost is the island you know today as Manhattan. While the Dutch secured their monopoly through violence, the VOC itself was becoming something the world had never seen before. It wasn't just a trading company. It could mint its own currency, sign its own treaties with foreign rulers, build its own forts, and maintain its own private army and navy, at times larger than many national forces of the era. It could declare war on a local kingdom on Tuesday and be negotiating a trade deal with a different one by Friday, all without ever consulting the government back in the Netherlands. Shareholders in Amsterdam collected enormous returns while rarely asking too many questions about how those returns were generated on the other side of the world. A pattern that would repeat itself in colonial ventures for centuries afterward. [music] Historians now call it the first true multinational corporation. A private company with the legal power to wage war, colonize territory, and administer justice [music] over conquered populations. Nutmeg, mace, and cloves were the fuel that built it, and Bander was the proof of concept for exactly how far the company was willing to go to protect [music] that fuel supply. If you're finding this one interesting, stick around because the story only gets darker from here. And the next part is the piece of Nutmeg's history that most documentaries choose to leave out entirely. For the survivors of the Bander massacre, the horror didn't end [music] with the killing. Those who weren't executed were shackled and shipped to Dutch controlled Betavia as forced laborers, crammed into ships where disease spread unchecked, [music] and many never survived the voyage at all. Contemporary Dutch accounts written by the perpetrators themselves describe villages left completely empty, cooking fires still smoldering, fields abandoned mid-h harvest, and the few remaining Bandenees so traumatized that some chose to leap from cliffs [music] into the sea rather than be taken. Eight of the most influential island leaders were sealed inside bamboo cages and executed in public by Japanese mercenaries [music] hired for the purpose. their bodies cut into pieces as a warning to anyone still resisting. Dozens more were beheaded, their heads mounted on bamboo poles and displayed around the fort. Out of an original population near 15,000, fewer than 1,000 Bandines remained on the islands within a year. An entire culture, its language, its trading networks, its way of life was reduced to a footnote almost overnight. All to secure control of a spice that today sells for pocket change at any grocery store on Earth. For centuries, almost nobody outside the Netherlands even knew this had happened. Cohen returned home celebrated, not condemned, promoted, wealthy, and eventually appointed Governor General a second time, dying in office, still regarded by the company as one of its most effective servants. It took nearly 200 years before Dutch and European historians began seriously reckoning with what he had done on Bander, eventually attaching him the nickname that stuck in the history books, the butcher of Bander. Even then, resistance to that reckoning ran deep. A large bronze statue of Cohen stood proudly in the central square of his hometown of Horn for generations, defended for years by local officials who argued he was simply a man of his time, doing what commerce demanded, and who pointed to the wealth his conquests had brought the wider Dutch Republic as some kind of justification. It took [music] sustained pressure from historians, descendants of the Bandanese diaspora scattered [music] across Indonesia and repeated public protest before that legacy was seriously [music] confronted at all. In 2020, the Dutch king issued a formal apology for colonial era violence committed across the former Dutch East Indies, Bander included, nearly 400 years after Cohen's fleet first arrived. An apology that many descendants of the band diaspora [music] said was long overdue and still incomplete. The Dutch monopoly itself finally cracked. Not through justice, but through theft. In 1770, a French horiculturalist named Pierre Puavra successfully smuggled nutmeg seedlings [music] out of VOCC territory and transplanted them on the French controlled island of Mauritius off the coast of East Africa. It was the first successful break in two centuries of total Dutch control, achieved not by an army or a navy, but by a single determined botonist willing to risk his life on repeated [music] failed attempts before one finally worked. From Maitius, nutmeg cultivation spread further to Zanzibar to Salon and eventually in 1843 to a small Caribbean island called Granada, more than 15,000 miles from where the very first tree had ever grown wild. The monopoly nature had created by accident, and the Dutch had defended with genocide was finally deliberately broken by human hands, one smuggled seedling at a time. From there, Nutmeg's transformation was almost anticlimactic. What had once justified genocide and empire slowly became one more spice on a supermarket shelf, it found its way into eggnog, pumpkin pie, mold wine, and holiday baking across the Western world. Worked into cuisines from the Caribbean to the Middle East to South Asia. standardized, regulated, [music] and traded as an ordinary agricultural commodity rather than a strategic asset [music] worth going to war over. Government food safety agencies now set maximum allowable limits for it in processed food. Import duties replaced naval blockades. Commodity exchanges replaced armed convoys. The same spice that once required a private army to protect now moves through the world in shipping containers alongside black pepper and cinnamon tracked [music] by customs codes instead of company monopoly charters. Bought and sold in bulk by buyers who have likely never heard the name Yan Peterun Cohen at all. But nutmeg's reputation carried baggage the marketing never mentioned. For centuries, Europeans believed carrying nutmeg warded off the plague, wearing it in small pouches around the neck as [music] protection against the black death. And physicians of the era prescribed it for everything from stomach ailments to melancholy to what they delicately called disorders of passion, treating it almost as a cure all long before anyone understood what was actually inside it. It probably did nothing of the sort medically, though some historians note the pouches may have incidentally repelled the fleas that [music] actually carried the disease, giving the superstition just enough accidental truth to survive for generations and [music] get repeated as folk wisdom well into the modern era. What actually deserves scrutiny is a different, more modern claim that nutmeg is a safe, mild way to catch a buzz. It is not. In large doses, the compound myristin found in nutmeg is genuinely psychoactive, but the effective dose sits dangerously close to the toxic one with almost no safe middle ground. Forensic toxicology journals have documented specific cases of nutmeg poisoning causing hallucinations, racing heartbeat, seizures, and in rare instances, death. All from a spice sitting openly in kitchen cabinets. sold without warning labels, without age restrictions, without any of the regulation applied to substances with comparable effects. That gap between reputation and reality hasn't gone away. In recent years, a recurring trend, sometimes called the nutmeg challenge, has resurfaced online and in prisons, where inmates without access to other substances grind up cafeteria nutmeg packets, mix them with water, and drink the slurry in search of a legal high. The practice isn't new. Sailors and prisoners have experimented with it for well over a century, long before social media gave it a catchy [music] name and a new audience of curious teenagers. It rarely works the way they hope. What follows is usually hours of nausea, dizziness, dry mouth, and disorientation rather than any pleasant [music] effect, followed sometimes by a trip to the infirmary. Poison control centers report a steady trickle of cases every year. Mostly teenagers experimenting after finding the trend online, [music] discovering the hard way that the spice their grandmother used at Christmas, can put them in an emergency room. A commodity that European empires once fought wars over, worth more than its weight in gold, is now something health authorities have to actively warn people away from misusing. sitting unlocked and unregulated in almost every kitchen on Earth. Globally, the picture today is almost unrecognizable from the 17th century. Indonesia, the original source, remains one of the largest nutmeg producers on Earth. Alongside India, Sri Lanka, and Grenada, together supplying kitchens [music] on every continent. Where a single pound once traded for a small fortune, nutmeg now trades as an unglamorous [music] bulk commodity worth a tiny fraction adjusted for value of what it once commanded. Priced in tons rather than ounces of gold, supermarkets stock it year round without a second thought next to cinnamon and paprika. And most shoppers walking past it have no idea that a war was once fought over exactly this shelf space. The empire building potential nature accidentally built into 10 small volcanic islands has been permanently diffused by simple bot [music] spread thin across three continents and it will never again be concentrated in one place the way it was for those first two centuries no matter how much any [music] single company or nation might want it to be. Grenada in particular built its modern identity around the very spice that once nearly destroyed an entire people on the other side of the world. Locals call it black gold. The country calls itself the aisle of spice. And its national flag carries a nutmeg fruit stitched [music] directly into the design. Split open exactly like the ones Portuguese sailors first found on Bander 500 years earlier. A permanent symbol of the crop's importance to national identity and economy. For generations, nutmeg accounted for the vast majority of Grenada's agricultural exports and provided income to roughly a third of the island's population, an entire national economy, resting on a tree species that originally belonged to a completely different part of the world. Then in 2004, Hurricane Ivan tore across the island as a category 3 storm, flattening an estimated 90% of Granada's nutmeg trees in a single day alongside most of the country's homes, schools, and hospitals. Because a nutmeg tree takes 7 years or more to mature and bear fruit again, the island's signature industry didn't just suffer. It nearly vanished overnight. Even [music] a decade later, production remained a small fraction of what it had been before the storm. A reminder that the same geography that made nutmeg possible in the first place can just as easily take it away. No matter how many centuries of history a country has built on top of it, and what became of Run, the tiny island the Dutch valued more than Manhattan. Today, it remains part of Indonesia, a forgotten backwater accessible only by small boat, home to a few hundred people and old nutmeg groves growing quietly among the ruins of colonial forts reclaimed by jungle. Fishermen and nutmeg farmers still work the same volcanic soil that started the entire conflict. And mature trees on the island can still produce roughly a thousand fruits every 4 months, much as they did four centuries ago. A marble monument now marks the anniversary of the treaty that traded the island away. But there is no skyline, no global financial center, no 8 million residents, no subway system running [music] beneath the street. The two islands swapped in 1667 took the most opposite paths imaginable. And [music] the side that seemed like the losing trade at the time turned out to hold the future. So think about everything that came from 10 square miles of volcanic rock sitting quietly in the Bander Sea unknown to most of the world for most [music] of history. A trade network so lucrative that Arab merchants invented monster stories to hide it. Yan Peterson Cohen, a man so consumed by a 12-year grudge that he erased an entire civilization to [music] satisfy it. 15,000 bandines reduced to fewer than a thousand in under 10 weeks. A private company so powerful it minted its own coins and fought its own wars. A tiny island called Run traded for what would become the most valuable real estate on the planet. A French smuggler quietly ending two centuries of monopoly with a handful of stolen seedlings. A Caribbean nation that stitched the spice directly into its flag only to watch a single [music] hurricane destroy 90% of it in a day. a folk remedy against the plague that turned out to be almost entirely wrong and a modern myth about getting high that turns out to be genuinely dangerous. And somewhere in a kitchen, prisons and a poison control centers still have to warn people about today sits the very same spice in a small jar costing a few dollars that people once slaughtered each other over. Next time you shake a little nutmeg over your eggnog or your pumpkin pie, remember what it actually costs the world to get there.
